title: The Circadian Code
identity_check: DB book 1363 / list_no 163: tr 'Sirkadyen Kod', en 'The Circadian Code', Satchin Panda, year 2019 in DB. Rodale hardcover is dated June 2018 (paperback Feb 2020), so brief uses 2018; DB year 2019 left unchanged. No duplicate under another title in the DB.

facts.claim: Panda's group (Salk Institute) helped identify melanopsin, a blue-light-sensitive pigment in cells of the eye (intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells) that passes ambient light information to the brain's master clock. Science papers 2002, 2003, 2005.

One 2003 paper showed melanopsin is needed for the clock-and-light responses of blind mice; summaries of the book state the light-sensing protein works even in people who are blind or visually impaired.
Light is the most powerful time cue (zeitgeber) for the circadian rhythm, per the book summary.
Blue light at night suppresses melatonin and disrupts sleep; reducing night-time blue light and getting morning daylight help the rhythm re-synchronise.

Panda's 2015 app study (Gill and Panda, Cell Metabolism): over 150 healthy adults aged 21 to 55 in San Diego, not on a diet, photographed everything they ate and drank for three weeks; each photo was time-stamped.
Most participants ate across 15 hours or longer a day; less than a quarter of daily calories came before noon and over a third after 6 p.m.
The authors proposed that irregular meal timing causes 'metabolic jetlag', metabolic organs falling out of sync with the body's circadian rhythms.

Hatori et al. 2012 mouse study (Panda lab): two groups ate a diet with 60% of calories from fat; one ate whenever it wanted, the other only in an 8-hour window each night (about 16 hours fasting). After 100 days both ate the same calories; free-eating mice gained weight and developed high cholesterol, high blood glucose, liver damage and worse motor control; the restricted mice weighed 28% less and showed none of these effects.
Panda in 2012: 'we will have to wait for human studies to prove this'; co-author Megumi Hatori said there are bound to be limits to the protection.

Pilot with eight overweight people who ate over 14 hours a day: asked to eat within 10 to 11 hours with no other change. After 16 weeks they had lost weight, said they felt more energetic and slept better. Small pilot.
Panda cautioned that changing eating duration is not the only way to improve health and may be risky for people with undiagnosed fasting hypoglycemia.

App study details: participants were recruited through online and print ads in San Diego and had to visit the lab to sign consent; reminders went out about once a day; food data were not stored in the app. Photos recorded location and time.

Beyond meal timing the photos showed other patterns: nearly two-thirds of participants took supplements or vitamins, at times that varied from day to day, as did medication; coffee and milk in the morning, alcohol in the evening, tea throughout the day, yogurt as a morning food, sandwiches and burgers at lunch, vegetables and ice cream in the evening; chocolate and candy photos from about 10 a.m. onward.
The study had no shift-worker data; the authors said larger studies including shift workers are needed. They also noted that humans differ metabolically from small model animals.
Pilot participants kept a weekly 'feedogram' (chart of their eating pattern) during the 16 weeks.
Mouse control groups ate a standard diet with about 13% of calories from fat under similar conditions.

Panda has led a lab at the Salk Institute in San Diego since 2004; his group's melanopsin work is cited in research on light therapy for insomnia, ADHD and migraines; a 2019 Science paper described the functional diversity of human melanopsin cells.

rejected.claim: 2017 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (three scientists), every cell has a clock.
rejected.reason: Nobel is real but connection to the book not verified; left out.

rejected.claim: Orchestra / conductor metaphor (sunlight and meal timing as conductor).
Night-shift workers store more fat from the same food.
rejected.reason: Salk release says no shift-worker data in the app study; unverified.

rejected.claim: Mice study lasted 18 weeks and showed diabetes symptoms; 12-week human study with 10-hour window, blood pressure drop.
rejected.reason: Duration 100 days per ScienceDaily; the 16-week eight-person pilot is the verified human one; blood pressure and 12 weeks unverified.

rejected.claim: 200,000 years of firelight; 150 years of electric light; 20 years of phones; phone at 10 pm tricks brain.
IARC 2019 classifies night shift as 2A; shift workers' rates of insulin resistance and heart disease.
Light and screen changes measurably improved sleep within two weeks in Panda's work.

1585.note: Rebuilt on the 150-person app study and 'metabolic jetlag'. Nobel and orchestra items dropped.

1586.note: Mice: 100 days not 18 weeks. Eight-person pilot replaces the unverified 12-week study; caveats from Panda included.

1587.note: Thin: melanopsin mechanism only; no numbers from the book beyond published papers. Confidence low.
